en: The Sūtra on the Definitive Karmic Obstructions Spoken of the Sublime Dharma, translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Zhiyan of Zhixiang Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was dwelling in the Palace of the Treasury of the Dharma-realm, where all Buddhas assemble.
At the peripheral site of enlightenment, he was together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.
At that time, there was a lady at this site of enlightenment named Guṇavyūhapuṣpasaṃkusumitā; she joined her palms toward the Buddha and withdrew to sit to one side.
At that time, the lady addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If there is a bodhisattva who has newly begun their practice, what kind of person is not a good spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) and with whom one should not dwell?"
The Buddha told the lady:

"If, within the three realms, there are Brahmās, Śakras, the Four Kings, śramaṇas, or brāhmaṇas, they are all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) to a practicing bodhisattva; only śrāvakas are excluded as not being spiritual friends (for fear that śrāvakas might cause a practicing bodhisattva to regress from the Mahāyāna path)."

Why is this? Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, for the sake of their own benefit, urge and lead newly practicing Bodhisattvas to turn back and enter the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, those of the Śrāvaka vehicle are not spiritual friends.

"Good man, you should know that a bodhisattva who has first begun their practice should not dwell in the same quarters as a śrāvaka bhikṣu, nor sit upon the same seat, nor travel along the same path."

If a bodhisattva who has newly begun their practice possesses ever-expanding wisdom and has awakened to the Mahāyāna through non-dual discernment, they may, as a skillful means, exhort and lead śrāvakas to enter the Mahāyāna, and only then permit them to dwell together;
however, if a śrāvaka bhikṣu’s merit and wisdom are narrow and inferior, a practicing bodhisattva should not preach the profound Mahāyāna to them, for fear that they might slander it.
Furthermore, a practicing bodhisattva should not frequently peruse the sūtras and śāstras of the Hīnayāna. Why is this?
Because they act as obstacles to the Buddha-way.
"Good man, you should know that a practicing bodhisattva would rather sacrifice their own body and life than abandon *bodhi* to enter the path of the śrāvakas and seek the fruit of an arhat.

Once a bodhisattva has exhorted all sentient beings, if they then abandon the mind of *bodhi* and instead give rise to a divergent path by entering the fruits of the śrāvaka or arhat paths, the bodhisattva will regress from *bodhi* due to such affliction and confusion; both individuals shall fall together into the Avīci Hell."
The Buddha told the lady:
"A practicing bodhisattva would rather commit the five great transgressions, such as killing, than study for the fruit of a srotāpanna, provided they do not regress from their bodhisattva practice;

a bodhisattva would rather undergo the sufferings of hell for one kalpa, a hundred kalpas, or even a thousand kalpas, than study for the fruit of a sakṛdāgāmin, provided they do not regress from their bodhisattva practice."
A bodhisattva would rather fall among the animals than study for the fruit of an anāgāmin, so as not to regress from the practice of bodhi;
a bodhisattva would rather kill sentient beings and fall into hell than cultivate the fruit of an arhat, so as not to regress from bodhi.
The Arhat realizes [enlightenment] alone and enters parinirvāṇa privately, like a petty thief secretly entering another's house.

Because a practicing Bodhisattva embraces all sentient beings through the bodhicitta, they would rather dwell in a pit of fire than abide in the śrāvaka’s quiescent nirvāṇa; they do not retreat from bodhi. For this reason, it is for the sake of embracing sentient beings and causing them to enter the Buddha-way.

A bodhisattva who practices in this manner is revered by all the worlds—gods, humans, and asuras—and being worthy of offerings, they surpass the śrāvakas; thus, the retinues of māras and evil spirits are unable to cause them affliction or disturbance.
At that time, the lady addressed the Buddha, saying,
“Who are the retinues of the demonic māras?
The Buddha told the lady:

"In any place where Mahāyāna sūtras are expounded, if there are sentient beings who, upon hearing the teaching of the Mahāyāna, do not delight in hearing it but instead mock and slander it, you should know that they are the retinues of māras and evil spirits."

Because of the mental state of slandering the Mahāyāna sūtras, one dies and falls into the Avīci hell to undergo immeasurable suffering; subsequently, one is born as a hungry ghost who eats fire, excrement, and urine. After having exhausted such suffering throughout immeasurable kalpas, one is later born among humans, blind, deaf, mute, afflicted with leprosy, or physically incomplete.

After these beings have passed away, they will encounter a Tathāgata and personally receive his offerings only after immeasurable lifetimes; in the presence of those Buddhas, they shall again hear the Mahāyāna sūtras, which are pure and unadulterated.

At that time, the Tathāgata universally emitted sounds from all his pores; from each and every pore issued forth immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of dharma-rays, which further produced immeasurable verses of dharma-sound in praise.
At that time, if there were śrāvakas in this assembly, they would hear the Dharma of the Śrāvaka vehicle;
if there were those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, they would hear the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
and if there were practitioners of the Mahāyāna, they would hear the wondrous Dharma of the Mahāyāna.
Birds, beasts, and other such creatures each hear the Buddha-dharma according to their own sounds.
Among all the sentient beings in this assembly, those who in the past had never heard the Buddha-dharma with their ears all see the Tathāgata remaining silent and not speaking.

As for the other sentient beings, because they had previously slandered Mahāyāna sūtras, they fell into the hells or as hungry ghosts to undergo suffering for many kalpas; yet, at the time they slandered the Dharma, Mahāyāna entered their ears. Consequently, upon personally hearing the Mahāyāna from the Buddha, joy arose in their hearts, and they resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, ultimately achieving *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, the lady addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding this which you have called the Mahāyāna, for what reason is it named the Mahāyāna?
For what reason do you speak of it as the Mahāyāna?"
The Buddha said:
"O Lady! Excellent, excellent!"
The lady deeply delights in the Mahāyāna; for this reason, reflect well upon it, and I shall explain for you the names of the Mahāyāna.
That which causes people to take deep delight is called the Mahāyāna.
Second, immovability—this is called the Great Vehicle.
Third, faultlessness—this is called the Great Vehicle.
Fourth, immeasurability—this is called the Great Vehicle.
Fifth, it is like the four great oceans; this is called the Mahāyāna.
Sixth, it is revered by various classes of beings such as the garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas; this is called the Mahāyāna.
Seventh, it is praised by the gandharvas; this is called the Mahāyāna.
Eighth, it is revered by the devas; this is called the Mahāyāna.
Ninth, it is taken as a refuge by Brahmā; this is called the Mahāyāna.
Tenth, that which is revered by the Lord of Devas is called the Mahāyāna.
Eleventh, that which is embraced by the Four Kings is called the Mahāyāna.
Twelfth, that which is honored by the Dragon Kings is called the Mahāyāna.
Thirteenth, that which Bodhisattvas uphold and maintain is called the Mahāyāna.
Fourteenth, the accomplishment of Buddha-nature is called the Mahāyāna.
Fifteenth, that which the worthy and noble take refuge in is called the Mahāyāna.
Sixteenth, that which universally endures all that is received is called the Mahāyāna.
Seventeenth, that which is like the king of medicinal trees is called the Mahāyāna.
Eighteenth, the severing of all afflictions is called the Mahāyāna.
Nineteenth, the ability to turn the wheel of the Dharma is called the Mahāyāna.
Twentieth, being without words and without speech is called the Mahāyāna.
Twenty-first: having the characteristic of space is called the Mahāyāna.
Twenty-second: the lineage of the Three Jewels being uninterrupted is called the Mahāyāna.
Twenty-third: those sentient beings with dull faculties who lack faith—this is called the Mahāyāna.
Twenty-fourth: that which transcends all—this is called the Mahāyāna.

At that time, when the Buddha spoke the names and titles of the Great Vehicle’s majestic powers, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways; hundreds of thousands of musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; then, amidst the sky, the devas rained down flowers, and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sons of gods all resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta;
immeasurable hundreds of thousands of śrāvakas likewise all resolved upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Furthermore, those bodhisattvas who were at the stage of the first precept and had not yet awakened to the Dharma all attained awakening and understanding.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"What is the name of this Dharma?
How should it be upheld?
The Buddha said:
"This sutra is titled 'The Mahāyāna Guna-vaśī'; uphold it!
It is also titled 'The Exposition of the Definitive Karma-obstructions of the Sublime Dharma'; uphold it!"

When the Tathāgata had finished preaching this sutra, Ānanda, the Lady Guṇavyūhakusumitā, and all the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings were filled with great joy; they received, upheld, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sutra on the Definitive Karmic Obstructions Spoken of the Sublime Dharma.
